  -0.015) and median error -0.056 (-0.107 to -0.023), both real; within 15 minutes -0.068
  (-0.148 to -0.025); the blind lead-time blend -0.040. The first TSLM that beats the tabular
  baseline alone on data none of it had seen. (This September set is the combined-feature build
  with 32,553 test examples; its numbers are not comparable with the earlier 10,000 from
  `forward.parquet`, where XGBoost scored 3.244 / 2.586.)
- **Planned trajectory channels** (running time, dwell and minutes left per stop through the
  encoder, `examples_v5`): 3.604 / 2.879 against 3.606 / 2.878 without them. Nothing.

### Pending at the time of writing

- Long runs on the full test set: text plus encoder with the plain loss (started 00:50); text
  with the plain loss, 24,000 steps (01:06); text on the combined data and text plus encoder on
  the combined data with 72-hour series, both with the exact-minute plus CRPS loss (02:15).
- The September forward test of the 2,000-step text models and of the long runs.
- The plain 2,000-step checkpoint on the full 93,738-example test set.
- The main configuration at 12,000 steps, on an H100 and on the devbox, followed by the September
  forward test.

### Still open

- **TimeF export, resolved:** `add_tasks` re-collected every task and record id per call, so the
  export was quadratic (16k records in 57 s). Tasks now go through TimeNet's `set_task_stream`,
  and the exporter skips TimeNet's per-task record-id scan for task types without record
  references. The full dataset (298,430 records, 582,059 tasks, 88 MB) converts in 93 s and
  writes in 287 s, and TimeNet's `verify()` passes on the result.
- **Team backend bug:** injected job files are sent as plain text instead of base64.

## 17. What the literature says about tonight's findings

Checked against primary sources on 13 September, so the write-up can present the results as
corroborated rather than surprising.

- **Numbers as text is a known strong recipe.** LLMTime (Gruver, Finzi, Qiu, Wilson, NeurIPS 2023,
  arXiv:2310.07820) forecasts by writing the series as digit strings and finds tokenisation decides
  the outcome. Llama 3 tokenises every integer 0 to 999 as one token, which is exactly our answer
  space and our input regime (delays are small integers). Zhang et al. (arXiv:2504.08818) show
  learned tokenisers or encoders can overfit the training distribution and mask the backbone's
  own ability.
- **The extra time-series module is often dispensable.** Tan et al. ("Are Language Models Actually
  Useful for Time Series Forecasting?", NeurIPS 2024 spotlight, arXiv:2406.16964) find that removing
  or replacing the LLM-side adapter does not hurt, and pretrained parts do no better than from
  scratch; our "random encoder equals pretrained encoder" and "text beats encoder" results are the
  same shape. Qiu et al. (arXiv:2602.14744, 2026) argue the opposite on much larger data, so the
  claim is contested, not settled.
- **OpenTSLM's own text-only baseline** (Langer et al., arXiv:2510.02410) loses to the encoder by
  a few F1 points on short series (HAR) and only collapses on long ones (sleep staging, ECG with
  80k tokens). Our four series are short, so the encoder's advantage is not expected here; it
  buys memory and context, which this task does not need.
- **Horizon-dependent combination is standard forecasting practice** (Wang, Hyndman, Li, Kang,
  International Journal of Forecasting 2023; Cerqueira and Torgo, arXiv:2306.14563), with the
  warning that per-horizon weights overfit small calibration sets. Our five bucket weights are
  fitted on 3,000 validation examples and confirmed on 88,479 test examples.
- **Train delay prediction.** Published real-time MAEs of 0.5 to 2.5 minutes (Kecman and Goverde
  2015 on NS; Oneto et al. 2018 on RFI; Spanninger et al. 2022 review) come from short horizons on
  more punctual networks; the RIDE benchmark (Elliker et al., arXiv:2606.05070, Belgian network,
  temporal split) reports persistence 1.61, XGBoost 1.28 and graph networks 1.23 minutes MAE
  within 40 minutes, degrading to 4 to 5 minutes beyond 45, and calls persistence hard to beat by
  a wide margin. Our 3.4 minutes over horizons up to hours on a German summer with 60% long-distance
  punctuality is in the expected band; the per-lead-bucket numbers are the comparable ones.
  Probabilistic per-stop output with CRPS is rare (Spanninger, Wiedemann, Corman 2024 is the
  nearest), which is a fair novelty claim. Deutsche Bahn's own RI-Prognose publishes no delay
  error, only 74% accuracy on cancellation and platform-change announcements.
- **Data sanity.** Official 2025 punctuality (under 6 minutes): long-distance 60.1%, regional
  88.7%; H1 2026 long-distance 58.7% with 8% partly or fully cancelled. Our 25% late stops and 5%
  cancellations across all classes are consistent with that.

## Sources

- Challenge deck: Aionic Labs, "Temporal AI Challenge" (hackathon handout).
- Dataset: https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data and
  https://github.com/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data
- TimeNet catalog: https://docs.timenet.ai/catalog/datasets.html
- OpenTSLM checkpoints: https://huggingface.co/OpenTSLM
- bahnvorhersage.de method: https://bahnvorhersage.de/blog/time-histograms/ and
  https://gitlab.com/bahnvorhersage/bahnvorhersage
- Zugfinder: https://www.zugfinder.net/de/start
- RIS::Stations: https://developers.deutschebahn.com/db-api-marketplace/apis/product/ris-stations
- Llama mirror: https://huggingface.co/unsloth/Llama-3.2-3B

"""Fine-tune the trip-delay TSLM recipe on the db-route TimeNet datasets, one profile per GPU.

This is Jonas's training recipe (``db_delay/trip``: OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt on Llama-3.2-3B from the
published ``OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-3b-m4-sp`` encoder, LoRA on, a minute-distribution readout after
``Answer:``) pointed at our data instead of his. Nothing about the model is changed except that
``compute_loss`` no longer refuses an answer that is not a whole number of minutes: our records
carry four tasks, and the late/on-time, cause-family and traveller-sentence answers train as plain
token cross-entropy while the departure-delay task keeps his CRPS term on the minute token.

Multi-GPU is by profile, not by data parallelism: the backend launches a multi-GPU preset under
``torchrun``, and rank *i* trains profile *i* of ``--profiles`` on ``cuda:i`` with identical
steps, seed, batch and loss. The bake-off is the job. ``--profiles week`` on a one-GPU preset runs
a single profile the same way.

Inputs come from the bucket mount: ``/outputs/code/db_route.tar.gz`` (this repo's agents code) and
``/outputs/registry`` (the built TimeF datasets). Results go back with byte writes only under
``/outputs/runs/<tag>/<profile>/`` -- the mount refuses rename/chmod/utime.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import math
import os
import re
import shutil
import sys
import tarfile
import time
import types
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np

OUT = Path(os.environ.get("NEBIUS_OUTPUT_DIR", "/outputs"))
CODE = Path(os.environ.get("ROUTE_CODE", "/workspace/code"))
HF_HOME = Path(os.environ.get("HF_HOME", "/workspace/hf"))
PROFILE_IDS = {"week": "S", "quarter": "M", "season": "L", "multiscale": "XM"}
CELLS = ("val", "test_seen_entity", "test", "test_seen_time")
LEAKY = {"attributed_share", "artifact_bundle_sha", "split", "split_cell", "recency_weight"}


def log(rank: int, msg: str) -> None:
    print(f"[{time.strftime('%H:%M:%S')}][rank {rank}] {msg}", flush=True)


def wait_for(marker: Path, what: str, rank: int, minutes: int = 40) -> None:
    for _ in range(minutes * 6):
        if marker.exists():
            return
        time.sleep(10)
    raise SystemExit(f"rank {rank}: gave up waiting for {what}")


def stage(rank: int, tarball: Path) -> None:
    """Rank 0 unpacks the code and warms the model cache; the others wait on a marker."""
    marker = CODE / ".ready"
    if rank == 0:
        CODE.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        with tarfile.open(tarball) as tar:
            tar.extractall(CODE)
        from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download, snapshot_download  # noqa: PLC0415

        snapshot_download("unsloth/Llama-3.2-3B")
        hf_hub_download("OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-3b-m4-sp", "model_checkpoint.pt")
        marker.touch()
    else:
        wait_for(marker, "rank 0's staging", rank)
    features = CODE / "app" / "agents" / "src" / "features"
    for p in (features / "db_route", features / "db_delay" / "trip"):
        if str(p) not in sys.path:
            sys.path.insert(0, str(p))


def copy_tree_bytes(src: Path, dst: Path) -> int:
    n = 0
    for root, _dirs, files in os.walk(src):
        rel = Path(root).relative_to(src)
        (dst / rel).mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        for name in files:
            shutil.copyfile(Path(root) / name, dst / rel / name)
            n += 1
    return n


# --- samples ----------------------------------------------------------------


def caption_stats(captions: list[str]) -> list[float]:
    """The pre-normalisation mean and std the bridge writes into every caption: the level, for the baselines."""
    out: list[float] = []
    for text in captions:
        m = re.search(r"mean (-?[\d.]+) and std (-?[\d.]+)", text)
        out += [float(m.group(1)), float(m.group(2))] if m else [0.0, 0.0]
    return out


def build_rows(dataset, bridge) -> list[dict]:
    """Every (record, task) as a training sample with the fields the loop and the scorer need."""
    options: dict[str, set[str]] = {}
    for record in dataset.records:
        if bridge.annotation_map(record).get("split") != "train":
            continue
        for task in dataset.tasks_for(record):
            if type(task).__name__ == "ClassificationTask":
                options.setdefault(getattr(task, "target_schema", ""), set()).add(str(task.target))
    menus = {schema: tuple(sorted(values)) for schema, values in options.items()}

    rows: list[dict] = []
    for record in dataset.records:
        ann = bridge.annotation_map(record)
        scalars = {k: float(v) for k, v in ann.items()
                   if isinstance(v, (int, float)) and not isinstance(v, bool) and k not in LEAKY}
        for task in dataset.tasks_for(record):
            kind = type(task).__name__
            target = task.target
            y = None
            if kind == "ScalarPredictionTask":
                y = float(target)
                target = int(min(999, max(0, round(y))))  # one token: the readout's alphabet is 0..999
            proxy = types.SimpleNamespace(target=target, rationale=getattr(task, "rationale", None))
            row = bridge.BridgeRow(record, proxy)
            menu = menus.get(getattr(task, "target_schema", ""), ()) if kind == "ClassificationTask" else ()
            sample = bridge.build_sample(row, eos_token="", label_options=menu)
            sample["prefix"] = sample["answer"].rsplit(" Answer:", 1)[0] + " Answer:"
            sample.update(
                kind=kind, y=y, target_text=str(target), record_id=str(record.record_id),
                split=str(ann.get("split")), cell=str(ann.get("split_cell", ann.get("split"))),
                features=[*scalars.values(), *caption_stats(sample["time_series_text"])],
                feature_names=[*scalars.keys()] + [f"cap{i}" for i in range(2 * len(sample["time_series_text"]))],
            )
            rows.append(sample)
    return rows


def strip(sample: dict) -> dict:
    """Only the keys OpenTSLM's collate and the model read."""
    return {k: sample[k] for k in ("pre_prompt", "time_series_text", "time_series", "post_prompt", "answer", "prefix")}


# --- model ------------------------------------------------------------------


def make_model_class(TripTSLM, torch, F):
    class RouteTSLM(TripTSLM):
        """TripTSLM whose loss accepts any answer; the minute term applies where there is a minute."""

        def compute_loss(self, batch):
            eos = self.tokenizer.eos_token_id
            answers = [self.encode(s["answer"]) + [eos] for s in batch]
            embeds, mask, starts = self._assemble(batch, answers)
            hidden, head = self._hidden_and_head(embeds, mask)
            rows, cols, targets, num_rows, num_cols, num_targets = [], [], [], [], [], []
            for i, ids in enumerate(answers):
                minute_answer = len(ids) >= 3 and ids[-3] == self.space_id and ids[-2] in self.id_to_minute
                for j, token in enumerate(ids):
                    col = starts[i] + j - 1
                    at_minute = minute_answer and j == len(ids) - 2
                    if at_minute and self.loss_mode != "plain":
                        num_rows.append(i); num_cols.append(col); num_targets.append(self.id_to_minute[token])
                    if not (at_minute and self.loss_mode == "soft_crps"):
                        rows.append(i); cols.append(col); targets.append(token)
            dev = self.device
            logits = head(hidden[torch.tensor(rows, device=dev), torch.tensor(cols, device=dev)]).float()
            loss = F.cross_entropy(logits, torch.tensor(targets, device=dev))
            parts = {"token_ce": loss.item()}
            if num_rows:
                sel = head(hidden[torch.tensor(num_rows, device=dev), torch.tensor(num_cols, device=dev)]).float()
                y = torch.tensor(num_targets, device=dev, dtype=torch.float32)[:, None]
                cdf = torch.softmax(sel[:, self.minute_ids], dim=-1).cumsum(dim=-1)
                crps = ((cdf - (self.minutes[None] >= y).float()) ** 2).sum(dim=-1).mean()
                loss = loss + self.crps_weight * crps
                parts["crps"] = crps.item()
            self.last_parts = parts
            return loss

    return RouteTSLM


def lr_factor(step: int, warmup: int, total: int) -> float:
    if step < warmup:
        return (step + 1) / warmup
    progress = min(1.0, (step - warmup) / max(1, total - warmup))
    return 0.1 + 0.9 * 0.5 * (1 + math.cos(math.pi * progress))


# --- scoring ----------------------------------------------------------------


def score_scalar(y: np.ndarray, q: np.ndarray, probs: np.ndarray, metrics) -> dict:
    median = q[:, 9]  # LEVELS[9] == 0.5
    late_true = y >= 5
    p_late = probs[:, 5:].sum(axis=1) / probs.sum(axis=1)
    return {
        "n": int(len(y)),
        "median_error": float(np.abs(median - y).mean()),
        "crps": float(metrics.crps_from_quantiles(y, q).mean()),
        "coverage_10_90": float(((y >= q[:, 1]) & (y <= q[:, 17])).mean()),
        "width_10_90": float((q[:, 17] - q[:, 1]).mean()),
        "brier_late5": float(((p_late - late_true) ** 2).mean()),
        "late5_rate": float(late_true.mean()),
    }


def baselines(train: list[dict], cell_rows: list[dict]) -> dict:
    """Persistence (the entity's eight-week habit) and gradient boosting on the same scalars."""
    y = np.array([r["y"] for r in cell_rows])
    out: dict = {"n": int(len(y))}
    names = train[0]["feature_names"]
    idx = names.index("habit_median_delay_8w") if "habit_median_delay_8w" in names else None
    if idx is not None:
        habit = np.array([r["features"][idx] for r in cell_rows])
        out["persistence_median_error"] = float(np.abs(habit - y).mean())
    try:
        import xgboost as xgb  # noqa: PLC0415

        X = np.array([r["features"] for r in train]); Y = np.array([r["y"] for r in train])
        Xc = np.array([r["features"] for r in cell_rows])
        model = xgb.XGBRegressor(objective="reg:absoluteerror", n_estimators=400, max_depth=6,
                                 learning_rate=0.05, subsample=0.8, colsample_bytree=0.8, n_jobs=8)
        model.fit(X, Y)
        out["xgboost_median_error"] = float(np.abs(model.predict(Xc) - y).mean())
        qs = {}
        for level in (0.1, 0.5, 0.9):
            m = xgb.XGBRegressor(objective="reg:quantileerror", quantile_alpha=level, n_estimators=300,
                                 max_depth=6, learning_rate=0.05, subsample=0.8, n_jobs=8)
            m.fit(X, Y); qs[level] = m.predict(Xc)
        out["xgboost_coverage_10_90"] = float(((y >= qs[0.1]) & (y <= qs[0.9])).mean())
    except Exception as exc:  # noqa: BLE001
        out["xgboost_error"] = str(exc)[:200]
    return out


# --- main -------------------------------------------------------------------


def main() -> int:
    ap = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    ap.add_argument("--profiles", default="week,quarter,season,multiscale")
    ap.add_argument("--registry", default=str(OUT / "registry"))
    ap.add_argument("--tag", default=os.environ.get("RUN_TAG", "route"))
    ap.add_argument("--steps", type=int, default=2000)
    ap.add_argument("--batch-size", type=int, default=8)
    ap.add_argument("--eval-batch-size", type=int, default=16)
    ap.add_argument("--lr", type=float, default=1e-4)
    ap.add_argument("--lr-encoder", type=float, default=2e-4)
    ap.add_argument("--loss-mode", default="plain_crps", choices=["plain", "plain_crps", "soft_crps"])
    ap.add_argument("--eval-limit", type=int, default=600, help="scalar rows scored per cell")
    ap.add_argument("--generate", type=int, default=64, help="classification rows generated per cell")
    ap.add_argument("--save-every", type=int, default=500)
    ap.add_argument("--max-hours", type=float, default=2.5)
    ap.add_argument("--seed", type=int, default=0)
    ap.add_argument("--grad-checkpointing", action="store_true")
    args = ap.parse_args()

    rank = int(os.environ.get("LOCAL_RANK", "0"))
    profiles = [p for p in args.profiles.split(",") if p]
    if rank >= len(profiles):
        print(f"rank {rank}: no profile assigned, exiting", flush=True)
        return 0
    profile = profiles[rank]
    os.environ.setdefault("HF_HOME", str(HF_HOME))
    stage(rank, OUT / "code" / "db_route.tar.gz")

    import torch  # noqa: PLC0415
    import torch.nn.functional as F  # noqa: PLC0415
    from opentslm.model_config import PATCH_SIZE  # noqa: PLC0415
    from opentslm.time_series_datasets.util import extend_time_series_to_match_patch_size_and_aggregate  # noqa: PLC0415
    from timenet.client import TimeNet  # noqa: PLC0415

    import bridge  # noqa: PLC0415  (db_route)
    import metrics  # noqa: PLC0415  (db_delay/trip)
    from model import START_CHECKPOINT, TripTSLM  # noqa: PLC0415  (db_delay/trip)

    torch.cuda.set_device(rank)
    device = f"cuda:{rank}"
    torch.manual_seed(args.seed)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(args.seed)
    local = Path("/workspace/results") / profile
    local.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

    dataset_id = f"error404/db-route-{profile}"
    t = time.time()
    dataset = TimeNet(args.registry).load(dataset_id)
    rows = build_rows(dataset, bridge)
    train = [r for r in rows if r["split"] == "train"]
    by_cell = {c: [r for r in rows if r["cell"] == c] for c in CELLS}
    log(rank, f"{dataset_id}: {len(rows)} samples, train {len(train)}, "
              + ", ".join(f"{c} {len(v)}" for c, v in by_cell.items()) + f" ({time.time() - t:.0f}s)")

    RouteTSLM = make_model_class(TripTSLM, torch, F)
    model = RouteTSLM.from_opentslm_checkpoint(START_CHECKPOINT, loss_mode=args.loss_mode, device=device)
    if not model.lora_enabled:
        model.enable_lora()
    if args.grad_checkpointing:
        model.llm.gradient_checkpointing_enable(gradient_checkpointing_kwargs={"use_reentrant": False})

    def collate(batch: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
        batch = [strip(s) for s in batch]
        return extend_time_series_to_match_patch_size_and_aggregate(batch, patch_size=PATCH_SIZE)

    # -- train
    total, warmup = args.steps, max(10, int(0.03 * args.steps))
    groups = [{"params": list(model.encoder.parameters()) + list(model.projector.parameters()), "lr": args.lr_encoder},
              {"params": model.get_lora_parameters(), "lr": args.lr}]
    base = [g["lr"] for g in groups]
    opt = torch.optim.AdamW(groups, weight_decay=1e-2)
    trainable = [p for g in groups for p in g["params"]]
    model.train()
    started, step, window, skipped, run_log = time.time(), 0, [], 0, []
    order = rng.permutation(len(train))
    cursor = 0
    while step < total and time.time() - started < args.max_hours * 3600:
        if cursor + args.batch_size > len(order):
            order, cursor = rng.permutation(len(train)), 0
        batch = collate([train[i] for i in order[cursor:cursor + args.batch_size]])
        cursor += args.batch_size
        for g, b in zip(opt.param_groups, base):
            g["lr"] = b * lr_factor(step, warmup, total)
        try:
            loss = model.compute_loss(batch)
            loss.backward()
        except torch.OutOfMemoryError:
            opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True); torch.cuda.empty_cache(); skipped += 1
            log(rank, f"skipped an OOM batch ({skipped} so far)")
            continue
        torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(trainable, 1.0)
        opt.step(); opt.zero_grad(set_to_none=True)
        window.append({"loss": float(loss)} | model.last_parts)
        step += 1
        if step % 25 == 0:
            mean = {k: round(float(np.mean([w[k] for w in window if k in w])), 4) for k in window[-1]}
            el = time.time() - started
            log(rank, f"{profile} step {step}/{total} {mean} {el:.0f}s ({el / step:.2f}s/step)")
            run_log.append({"step": step, "seconds": round(el, 1)} | mean); window = []
        if step % args.save_every == 0:
            model.store_to_file(str(local / "checkpoint.pt"))
    model.store_to_file(str(local / "checkpoint.pt"))
    log(rank, f"{profile}: trained {step} steps in {time.time() - started:.0f}s, {skipped} skipped")

    # -- evaluate
    model.eval()
    results: dict = {"profile": profile, "dataset_id": dataset_id, "steps": step, "args": vars(args), "cells": {}}
    train_scalar = [r for r in train if r["kind"] == "ScalarPredictionTask"]
    for cell, cell_rows in by_cell.items():
        scalar = [r for r in cell_rows if r["kind"] == "ScalarPredictionTask"]
        if not scalar:
            continue
        if len(scalar) > args.eval_limit:
            scalar = [scalar[i] for i in sorted(rng.choice(len(scalar), args.eval_limit, replace=False))]
        probs = []
        with torch.no_grad():
            for i in range(0, len(scalar), args.eval_batch_size):
                batch = collate(scalar[i:i + args.eval_batch_size])
                try:
                    out = model.predict_distribution(batch)
                except torch.OutOfMemoryError:
                    torch.cuda.empty_cache()
                    out = {"probs": torch.cat([model.predict_distribution([s])["probs"] for s in batch])}
                probs.append(out["probs"].float().cpu().numpy())
        probs_np = np.concatenate(probs).astype(np.float64)
        q = metrics.quantiles_from_distribution(probs_np)
        y = np.array([r["y"] for r in scalar])
        entry = {"tslm": score_scalar(y, q, probs_np, metrics), "baselines": baselines(train_scalar, scalar)}
        np.savez_compressed(local / f"scalar_{cell}.npz", y=y, quantiles=q,
                            record_id=np.array([r["record_id"] for r in scalar]))
        # classification tasks: generate and parse
        for kind in ("ClassificationTask",):
            cls_rows = [r for r in cell_rows if r["kind"] == kind]
            if not cls_rows or not args.generate:
                continue
            pick = [cls_rows[i] for i in sorted(rng.choice(len(cls_rows), min(args.generate, len(cls_rows)), replace=False))]
            hits, majority = 0, {}
            for r in [x for x in train if x["kind"] == kind]:
                majority[r["target_text"]] = majority.get(r["target_text"], 0) + 1
            with torch.no_grad():
                for i in range(0, len(pick), 8):
                    chunk = pick[i:i + 8]
                    texts = model.generate_answers(collate(chunk), max_new_tokens=48)
                    for r, text in zip(chunk, texts):
                        answer = text.rsplit("Answer:", 1)[-1].strip().split()[0].strip(".") if "Answer:" in text else ""
                        hits += answer == r["target_text"]
            top = max(majority, key=majority.get) if majority else ""
            entry["classification"] = {"n": len(pick), "accuracy": hits / len(pick),
                                       "majority_class_accuracy": sum(r["target_text"] == top for r in pick) / len(pick)}
        results["cells"][cell] = entry
        log(rank, f"{profile} {cell}: {json.dumps(entry)}")
    results["train_log"] = run_log
    (local / "metrics.json").write_text(json.dumps(results, indent=2))
    dest = OUT / "runs" / args.tag / profile
    n = copy_tree_bytes(local, dest)
    log(rank, f"{profile}: copied {n} files to {dest}")
    return 0


if __name__ == "__main__":
    raise SystemExit(main())

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://docs.timenet.ai/schemas/dataset-card-v1.schema.json
# Dataset card for error404/db-route-multiscale: one of four sibling profiles built by one connector body
# (see ../db_route/pipeline.py). Same entities, anchors, labels and split in all four; only the
# history preceding each anchor differs. Every record carries artifact_bundle_sha to prove it.
yaml_schema_version: 1
dataset_id: error404/db-route-multiscale
dataset_version: 0.1.0
name: DB Route (multiscale)
description: >-
  The operational week at hourly resolution plus the same service and station at six-hourly over sixty days and daily over 120, on one record with three time axes. One record is one Deutsche Bahn service group at one station on one
  travel date; targets are next-week departure delay, a five-minute lateness flag,
  the dominant IRIS cause family, and a one-sentence traveller action. Dated
  disruption notices are attached as interval annotations. Profile XM, bucket 1h+6h+1d, span 7d+60d+120d.
license: CC-BY-4.0
domains:
  - transport
tags:
  - rail
  - delay
  - deutsche-bahn
  - cause-attribution
  - profile:XM
  - bucket:1h+6h+1d
  - span:7d+60d+120d
source_url: https://huggingface.co/datasets/piebro/deutsche-bahn-data
citation: >-
  Derived from piebro/deutsche-bahn-data (CC BY 4.0), an archive of the Deutsche
  Bahn Timetables API. Cause codes and disruption notices are parsed from the
  archived raw IRIS XML.
"""Timeline profiles: how much history one training sample sees.

**This module is a frozen contract.** Everything downstream reads it and nothing
else knows about timescale, so a profile is a config object rather than a code
path. Adding a fifth profile is a tuple literal, not a branch.

Delay causes live at different timescales -- rush hour is daily, construction is
monthly, weather is seasonal -- so the pipeline emits sibling datasets that
differ *only* in how much history precedes the anchor, and held-out cells pick
the winner. Same anchors, same labels, same splits, same tasks, same seed.

Two constraints set the ladder, and they are not the same constraint:

* **The hard cap.** OpenTSLM refuses a series longer than 4096 samples
  (1024 patches x patch_size 4) -- it raises rather than truncating. Hourly
  therefore tops out at 170 days.
* **Timetable churn, which bites first.** Germany's Fahrplanwechsel is every
  December; construction schedules shift; demand moved with the Deutschlandticket.
  A 364-day window straddles a timetable change and so partly describes a network
  that no longer exists. 60-180 days is the band where history is still about
  *this* network.

Every ``n_steps`` below is divisible by 4, so no series is ever right-zero-padded.
That matters more than it sounds: OpenTSLM pads to a multiple of the patch size
and carries **no padding mask**, so padding is indistinguishable from data.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from fractions import Fraction

# The six canonical signals. Every profile draws from this set; a layer picks a
# subset. Names are stable -- they become the ``signal`` on a TimeNet TimeSeries
# and the key of the caption annotation the bridge reads.
SIGNALS: tuple[str, ...] = (
    "service_delay",  # mean delay of this service group across its stops
    "station_delay",  # mean delay of all trains at this station (congestion)
    "station_cancel_rate",  # cancellation rate at this station
    "service_at_station_delay",  # this service AT this station -- the specific habit
    "station_throughput",  # stop-event count at this station
    "service_throughput",  # stop-event count for this service group network-wide
    "works_share",  # share of attributed delay minutes from the `works` family
)

# Cause-family shares carried only at the coarser layers. At 7 days they are too
# sparse to be anything but noise; at 60+ they are how a regime shift becomes
# visible, which is the whole point of the long profiles.
CAUSE_SIGNALS: tuple[str, ...] = (
    "weather_share",
    "technical_share",
    "knock_on_share",
    "attributed_share",
)

_SECONDS = {"1 hour": 3600, "6 hours": 21600, "1 day": 86400}

# OpenTSLM's encoder positional table is 1024 patches at patch_size 4.
MAX_SAMPLES = 4096
PATCH_SIZE = 4


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class Layer:
    """One (bucket, span) view of history, and the signals drawn at that scale."""

    layer_id: str  # "week" | "quarter" | "season"
    bucket: str  # a DuckDB INTERVAL literal, key of _SECONDS
    n_steps: int
    signals: tuple[str, ...]

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if self.bucket not in _SECONDS:
            raise ValueError(f"unknown bucket {self.bucket!r}; expected one of {sorted(_SECONDS)}")
        if self.n_steps % PATCH_SIZE:
            raise ValueError(
                f"{self.layer_id}: n_steps={self.n_steps} is not divisible by {PATCH_SIZE}, so the "
                f"collate would right-zero-pad it -- and there is no padding mask to tell the "
                f"encoder which values are real"
            )

- **Stacking is the oldest combination recipe; an LLM as the second stage is new.** Wolpert
  (Neural Networks 1992) and Breiman ("Stacked regressions", Machine Learning 1996) fit the
  second stage on out-of-fold predictions of the first, which is why XGBoost's forecast in the
  training prompts is out-of-fold. Bates and Granger (1969) and the M4 competition (Makridakis
  et al., IJF 2018: 12 of the 17 most accurate methods were combinations) say combining beats
  either forecaster alone. The nearest LLM work is CorDP (Ashok et al., TMLR 2026,
  arXiv:2508.09904): an LLM is handed a probabilistic forecast from Chronos, Lag-Llama or ARIMA
  and corrects it, beating the base forecaster in 11 of 13 models on the Context is Key benchmark
  (Williams et al., ICML 2025, arXiv:2410.18959); the two failures are the smallest models (1B and
  1.5B), and none is fine-tuned. We found no published case of a fine-tuned 3B model trained on
  out-of-fold base forecasts, which is what the stacked TSLM is, and its blend weight of 1.0 is
  the expected outcome once the second stage already contains the first.

<result>I did not check out the branch or edit anything. Most of the db_route pipeline is already on main; the branch only adds `train_route.py`, which runs our TripTSLM on their datasets.

**1. Record and target: aggregated, not per train run**
- The entity is a (service group, station) pair. Service group is `train_type -> final_destination_station`, not a line number (`sources.py:SERVICE_GROUP_SQL`, `entities.py`).
- One record is one entity at one anchor, where the anchor is a travel date at 00:00 local. Each entity gets 5 anchors, 35 days apart (`anchors.py`).
- The horizon is the 7 days after the anchor (`anchors.py:horizon_of`, `profiles.HORIZON_DAYS=7`).
- The departure-delay `ScalarPredictionTask` target is `avg(delay_in_min)` over every stop of that service group at that station in those 7 days (`labels.py:_horizon_rows`, `connector.py:_tasks_for`). The prompt asks how late it will be "over the coming week".
- `delay_in_min` is the departure delay, not arrival. Cancelled stops are not in the target.
- Each record has three more tasks: late ≥5 min (the weekly mean thresholded), the dominant cause family, and a one-sentence traveller answer.

**2. Profiles** (`profiles.py`)
- **week (S):** hourly buckets over 7 days, 168 steps.
- **quarter (M):** 6-hour buckets over 60 days, 240 steps.
- **season (L):** daily buckets over 120 days, 120 steps.
- **multiscale (XM):** all three layers, with fewer signals on the two coarse ones.
- Signals are service, station and pair delay, cancel rate, throughput, and cause-family shares.
- Buckets are rebuilt from an hourly cache of sums and counts, not averages (`resample.py`, `facts.py`). All four profiles share the same anchors and labels.

**3. Splits**
- `plan_anchors(split_mode="both")` (pipeline.py) cuts time at anchor-date quantiles (70/15/15) and also holds out 30% of entities.
- `test_seen_entity` = later dates, known entity. `test_seen_time` = earlier dates, unseen entity. `test` = both held out.
- A 7-day purge sits only at the time boundaries. Their own comment says context windows still overlap training labels.
- Leakage issues I found:
  - `attributed_share` is computed from the horizon. `train_route.LEAKY` correctly excludes it.
  - `habit_median_delay_8w` is never filled in: `CONTEXT_SLOTS` doesn't have it and only a test fixture sets it. So the persistence baseline in `train_route.baselines` silently doesn't run.
  - Notices are filtered on validity dates but not on `issued_at` (`pipeline.py:_notices_for`), so a notice published after the anchor can get in.

**4. Causes**
- They come from the raw IRIS XML `<m>` elements in piebro `raw_data` (`fchg` responses) via `causes.py:parse_stops`. There are two kinds:
  - **Cause codes** (types d/f/q, field `c`): mapped to German text (`CAUSE_TEXT`) and 6 families. Stored per stop as `stop_id, codes, families`. `stop_id` equals the processed parquet's `id` (`ride_id-YYMMDDHHmm-stop_number`), so it is per train run, per stop, per day.
  - **Planned-disruption notices** (type h): `category` (e.g. Bauarbeiten), `valid_from/to`, `priority`, `issued_at`, and a list of stop ids.
- In db_route they are only summed into weekly shares and notice intervals per station.
- The cause codes have no timestamp. They are the final archived state, so they are only known after the fact.
- **Joining onto our examples:**
  - Yes, exactly, on piebro `id`.
  - To be safe at forecast time, only use codes from stops whose planned time is before the forecast time: earlier stops of the same run, or earlier trains on the route.
  - Notices can be filtered properly with `issued_at <= forecast time` and a validity window covering the target stop, per station.
  - The shards only cover 2025-11-02 to 2026-08-31 (`remote_extract.py`), so our September out-of-time set has no causes unless we extract more.

**5. Data source:** the same piebro/deutsche-bahn-data (processed monthly files plus `raw_data`).

- The Nebius build is all of Germany, 2025-11 to 2026-08, 3000 entities (`remote_build.py`).

- **Different problem:** the weekly service-group mean target, the TimeF connectors and bridge, the profile bake-off, and `train_route.py`. The same goes for their metrics: they aren't comparable to our per-train CRPS.</result>

# Should we use the `feat/db-route-multiscale` branch?

**No, not for the submission model.** It solves a different problem, and wiring in its useful part would not pay off before 12:00.

**Why it doesn't fit:**
- **What it predicts:** one record is one service group (train type plus destination) at one station. The target is the mean departure delay over the next 7 days. We predict one specific train's arrival, minutes to hours ahead, as a distribution. Their scores can't be compared with ours.
- **What `train_route.py` is:** our trip recipe pointed at their datasets, not a new method. Their first run (`route-bakeoff-2k`, submitted 04:22) is still waiting for a GPU, so there are no results yet.
- **Merging:** it merges cleanly with our branch and touches no `db_delay` file, so it doesn't block us either way.

**What would be worth using:** the cause data, which is the "cause text" feature we had wanted.
- `causes.py` parses delay-cause codes (construction, weather, technical, knock-on) and planned-works notices from the raw DB XML.
- The codes are stored per train, per stop, per day, keyed on the same `id` as our parquet, so they would join exactly.
- To avoid leakage we could only use causes from stops before the forecast time: earlier stops of the same train, or earlier trains on the route. The codes carry no timestamp; they are the final archived state.

**Why not now:**
1. Their cause extraction ends on 31 August, so our September test would have no causes until someone extracts September.
2. We would have to rebuild the examples, retrain (about 2 hours for 12,000 text steps), and re-run the full test and September before 12:00. The stacked model already beats XGBoost everywhere, and swapping it out this late is the bigger risk.
3. We still don't have access to their cause files in their bucket.

**Worth telling your teammate before they present numbers:**
- **Leak:** notices are filtered by validity dates but not by publication date, so a notice published after the anchor date can reach the input.
- **Silent baseline:** `habit_median_delay_8w` is never filled in, so the persistence baseline in `train_route.py` is skipped without an error.
- **Overlap:** the 7-day purge sits only at the time boundaries. Their own comment says history windows still overlap training labels.

**What I'd do instead:** mention their TimeNet connectors and the cause extraction in our write-up as a joint contribution (TimeNet connectors are a challenge bonus), and name "causes known before the forecast time" as the next feature. If their cause files turn up in the next hour, a 2,000-step comparison on the May data is feasible, but it can't be tested on September.

Meanwhile our jobs are on track:
- `text-24k` has finished training and is scoring (about 05:30).
- `final-both` is due around 04:55.
- The September test of the combined-data text+encoder model on the devbox is nearly done.

I also added a stacking paragraph with checked sources to DESIGN §17; it isn't committed yet. The closest published work is CorDP (arXiv:2508.09904): an LLM that corrects a statistical forecast, zero-shot and not fine-tuned.

Goal: find out, with one short experiment, whether a teammate's delay-cause data improves our train-delay TSLM. Timebox: report back by 07:00 Europe/Zurich at the latest (check `TZ=Europe/Zurich date`; it is about 04:40 now). A clear "not feasible because X" early is a good result; do not burn hours.

## Repo and branches
- Main checkout: /Users/jonasstenglein/OtherProjects/EHL_Zurich/temporal_ai_error404.ai (do NOT edit files there, do not touch branch db-train-model, the owner is using it). You run in a git worktree; create a new local branch `try-route-causes` from `db-train-model` and `git merge origin/feat/db-route-multiscale` into it (already fetched; merge is conflict-free). Never push, never open a PR. Commit on your branch only, author `josteng <jonas@stenglein.dev>`, imperative subject, bullet body, message ending with `Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_018iVCQnxtrgxiBS2m9QW1F2`. Never commit anything under `.claude/`, data files, or `uv.lock`. No em dashes in any text you write. No real names/URLs/paths in committed docs or comments.
- Secrets: the S3 credentials live in the git-ignored `.env` at the main checkout root. `trip/nebius/sync_bucket.sh` reads `$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel)/.env`, so symlink that .env into your worktree root (it stays ignored). Never print the key, never copy it to the devbox.

## Our side (app/agents/src/features/db_delay/trip)
We predict one train's arrival delay (minutes, distribution 0..999 plus P(cancelled)) at one stop, from a forecast time 0 to hours ahead. Examples parquet files: `examples_v4.parquet` is the current best input (combined features plus an out-of-fold XGBoost forecast written into the per-example rationale sentence, see `stack.py` for how a sentence is added to the prompt, and `prompts.py`). Read `trip/README.md`, `stack.py`, `prompts.py` and the builder that makes examples to learn the columns (train run id / stop id, station, planned times, forecast time `lead`, split). Copies of the datasets: devbox `ssh devbox`, dir `~/Jonas/db_delay_tslm/data/trip/` (examples_v4.parquet, forward_v4.parquet) and the bucket under `data/` (use `bash trip/nebius/sync_bucket.sh ls`). The devbox GPU is BUSY with the owner's evaluations: do not run anything on the devbox GPU; light CPU work on the devbox is fine, and never `pkill -f`/`pgrep -f` there with a pattern that appears in your own ssh command.

## Their side (branch origin/feat/db-route-multiscale, dir app/agents/src/features/db_route)
`causes.py:parse_stops` parses the raw IRIS XML `<m>` messages from piebro/deutsche-bahn-data `raw_data` (fchg responses): cause codes (types d/f/q, field c, mapped to text and 6 families) stored per stop with `stop_id` equal to the processed parquet's `id` (`ride_id-YYMMDDHHmm-stop_number`), and planned-disruption notices (type h: category, valid_from/to, priority, issued_at, stop ids). `remote_extract.py` ran this on Nebius over 2025-11-02 to 2026-08-31 and wrote shards (reportedly `/outputs/causes/all` and `notices/all` in the teammate's bucket, which we may not be able to read). Check `remote_extract.py`, `pack_remote.py`, `facts.py` for where shards go and how extraction is launched.

## The experiment
1. Get cause data for the stops/dates our `examples_v4.parquet` covers (train and test splits; note which months): first try to locate the teammate's shards (their bucket via the nebius CLI `/Users/jonasstenglein/.nebius/bin/nebius storage bucket list` in the shared project, or our bucket); otherwise judge whether extracting ourselves is feasible within the timebox (raw_data size on Hugging Face, CPU time). If neither is feasible, stop and report.
2. Leakage rule (strict): cause codes carry no timestamp and are the final archived state, so only use codes of stops whose planned (or actual) time is before the example's forecast time: earlier stops of the same run, and trains at the target station / on the route in the preceding hours. Notices only if `issued_at <= forecast time` and the validity window covers the target stop time. Never the target stop's own codes.
3. Build `examples_v6.parquet` = examples_v4 plus one short cause sentence appended to the rationale (e.g. "Earlier stops of this train report: technical fault (2x). Construction notice active at this station."), empty when nothing. Report coverage (share of examples with a non-empty sentence, by split).
4. One smoke job on Nebius H100 mirroring the stacked 2k run `jonas-h100-v4-text`: generate the spec with `python trip/nebius/job_spec.py` (look at `tmp/nebius/job-h100-v4-text*.json` in the main checkout and the script's --help for the template and flags; timeout like `150m`, never `2h30m`), `--steps 2000 --test-limit 5000 --generate 16`, custom args `--loss-mode plain_crps --prompt-mode text --grad-checkpointing`, tag `h100-v6-causes`, job name must start with `jonas-`. Upload the dataset with `sync_bucket.sh put <file> data/examples_v6.parquet`. Submit with `cd app/backend && npm run train -- submit-spec <json>` and then verify it exists with `nebius ai job list --format json`. Exactly one job; if quota is full it may queue: that is fine, report the id. The Nebius CLI gotchas memory is at /Users/jonasstenglein/.claude/projects/-Users-jonasstenglein-OtherProjects-EHL-Zurich-temporal-ai-error404-ai/memory/nebius-cli-gotchas.md: read it first.
5. If the job finishes before your timebox, fetch results (`sync_bucket.sh results h100-v6-causes <dir>`) and compare with the stacked 2k run (5,000 shared test trips: median error 3.573, CRPS 2.860; validation 2.745 / 2.188) using `trip/bootstrap.py --a causes=<npz> --b stacked=<v4-text tslm_test.npz> --examples <examples_v6>`; the v4-text npz is in the main checkout under tmp/nebius/results/h100-v4-text/custom/ or on the devbox under out/trip/ablations/v4-text/. Otherwise just report the job id and ETA.

## Report (under 350 words)
What you merged (branch, commit), where the cause data came from, the leakage-safe feature definition, coverage by split, the job id / tag / state / ETA in Zurich time, and results if any, plus anything that blocked you.

    return ", ".join(f"{value:.0f}" for value in values)

def sample(row: pd.Series, text_only: bool = False, mode: str = "series", scaling: str = "z") -> dict:
    """One OpenTSLM sample, plus the answer prefix used to read out the distribution.

    ``mode`` decides how the four series reach the model: through the time-series encoder
    (``series``), written into the prompt as numbers with no encoder (``text``, the baseline;
    ``text_only`` is the same), or both at once (``both``).
    """
    if text_only:
        mode = "text"
    if mode not in MODES:
        raise ValueError(f"mode must be one of {MODES}, got {mode!r}")
    arrival = pd.Timestamp(row["k_arr_pt"])
    via = [v for v in as_list(row["via"]) if isinstance(v, str) and v]
    stop = name(row["k_station"])
    via_text = f" via {', '.join(via[:5])}{' and further stops' if len(via) > 5 else ''}" if via else ""
    where = (f"It has not departed from {name(row['first_station'])} yet." if row["pre_departure"]

    pre_prompt = (

        f"{name(row['origin'])} to {name(row['dest'])}. {where} Target stop: {stop}{via_text}, planned arrival "
        f"{WEEKDAYS[arrival.weekday()]} {arrival:%H:%M}."

    run = as_list(row["run_delays"])

    """A series-reading question with an exact numeric answer, for teaching the encoder to read.

    OpenTSLM trains its models in stages, captioning before the target task; this mixes the same
    idea into training. The series go through the encoder only, so the answer has to come from it.
    """
    base = sample(row, mode="series", scaling=scaling)
    stop = name(row["k_station"])
    run = [max(0.0, float(v)) for v in as_list(row["run_delays"])]
    station = np.asarray(row["station_series"], dtype=np.float64)
    network = np.asarray(row["network_series"], dtype=np.float64)
    hist = np.asarray(row["hist_series"], dtype=np.float64)
    questions = [
        (f"In how many of the last 24 hours were more than 20% of stops at {stop} late?", int((station[-24:] > 0.2).sum())),
        (f"What share of stops at {stop} were late in the most recent hour, in percent?", int(round(100 * station[-1]))),
        ("What share of stops nationwide were late in the most recent hour, in percent?", int(round(100 * network[-1]))),
        ("What was the median of the daily delay history, in whole minutes?", int(round(float(np.median(hist))))),
        ("What was the highest daily median delay in the history, in whole minutes?", int(round(float(hist.max())))),
    ]
    if run:
        questions += [

            ("What was the highest departure delay so far, in minutes?", int(round(max(run)))),
            ("From how many stops has the train departed so far?", len(run)),
            ("By how many minutes does the highest delay so far exceed the first, in minutes?", int(round(max(run) - run[0]))),
        ]
    question, answer = questions[seed % len(questions)]
    answer = min(max(answer, 0), 999)

Everything left is waiting on background jobs, so here is where things stand at 04:50 Zurich.

**Your question: can we show it?**
- **Better than the baseline: yes, today.** The stacked model beats XGBoost on the same features at every lead time: CRPS −0.075 on May test trips and −0.039 on unseen September data, both real. The full-test numbers (93,738 trips) come with the finals this morning.
- **Better than without the embeddings: no.** The encoder alone learns the task and beats XGBoost, but adding it to the model that reads the series as numbers changes nothing. A random encoder does as well as the pretrained one. I'd present embeddings and text as two routes to the same accuracy, with the embedding route the only one that scales to series too long for a prompt.
- **The ablation we were missing is now running.** `jonas-h100-none-plaincrps` is the same model with no time series at all, neither as text nor as embeddings; it was submitted at 04:46 and is still waiting for a GPU. Its partner is `text-plaincrps` (3.621 / 2.903 on the 5,000 shared test trips). If the gap is real, it shows the temporal signal matters beyond the summary numbers.

**New results**
- **Combined data without the XGBoost forecast (text plus encoder, 2k) on September:** 2.711 / 2.148 against XGBoost's 2.745 / 2.175.
  - Alone it is not a clear win: CRPS −0.028, interval −0.072 to +0.005.
  - It is a real win within 15 minutes (−0.071) and as a lead-time blend (−0.044).
  - So the stacked forecast sentence is what makes the model win out of time.
- **Committed `b314020`:** the no-series mode, this September result, and the DESIGN §17 paragraph on stacking with verified sources. Nothing is pushed.

**Running**
- **Teammate's causes:** a subagent is merging `feat/db-route-multiscale` in a separate worktree (local branch `try-route-causes`, not pushed). It is building examples with a leakage-safe cause sentence for one 2,000-step test job, and reports by 07:00.
- **Devbox:** the September test of the stacked 5,000-step model, done about 05:15.
- **Finals:**

  | `final-both` | ~04:55 |

Recorded and committed as `bfd56d9`:
- EVALUATION §5.2 now has the `final-both` full-test row.
- DESIGN §16 has a new Finals table.

The September test of `final-both` is queued on the devbox behind the stacked 5k test and should finish around 05:50. The no-series ablation is now running on Nebius.

One follow-up for later: EVALUATION §5.3 still says XGBoost wins beyond 30 minutes. That holds for the 2,000-step model only, so I'll rewrite it once all finals are in.

"| final-v4-both                           | ~08:15       |" how did that happen to take so long? And also check more encoder stuff. Aren't there other options. Maybe also some other tokenization or so or loss? Cause when the whole challenge is getting better embeds saying it is the same or worse is ... subideal

Two questions: why does `final-v4-both` take until 08:15, and what can make the embeddings actually matter? You're right that "same or worse" is a weak story for a TSLM challenge.

**Why 08:15.** It runs text plus encoder in one prompt, which needs gradient checkpointing to fit in memory. That puts it at 1.08 s per step (stacked text alone is 0.59, encoder alone 0.30). The job was submitted at 03:20:
- 12,000 steps take 3.6 hours;
- scoring all 93,738 test trips in that mode takes about an hour more.

It isn't the decision model: `final-v4-text` (~06:00) is.

**Encoder options worth running now:**
1. **What we compare against.** Text vs text plus encoder is the hardest test for the encoder: the text already carries the same numbers, so the encoder has nothing unique to add. The fair "with vs without embeddings" pair is **encoder only vs no series**. I'll run it on identical data, loss and steps.
2. **Modality dropout.** In text plus encoder mode, randomly hide the numbers from the prompt during training (say 50%). The model then has to learn to read the embeddings instead of ignoring them because the text is easier. This is a standard multimodal trick, a small code change and cheap to run.
3. **Efficiency.** Encoder only reaches the text model's accuracy with far fewer prompt tokens and half the step time. I'll measure prompt tokens per mode, which matches the brief's "context wall" slide.

To keep the jobs safe from the subagent overwriting the shared code in the bucket, I'll pin each job to its own copy of the code. First I'll read the training dataset code and the runner.

class TripDataset(Dataset):
    """Formats examples lazily, so large splits cost no upfront time."""

    def __init__(self, frame: pd.DataFrame, mode: str = "series", scaling: str = "z", caption_share: float = 0.0):
        self.frame = frame.reset_index(drop=True)
        self.mode = mode
        self.scaling = scaling
        self.caption_share = caption_share

    def __len__(self) -> int:
        return len(self.frame)

    def __getitem__(self, index: int) -> dict:
        row = self.frame.iloc[index]
        if self.caption_share > 0:
            # A fixed share of rows become series-reading questions, chosen by a hash so it is
            # reproducible and the same row is a question or a forecast in every epoch.
            draw = (int(row["example_id"]) * 2654435761) % 1000
            if draw < self.caption_share * 1000:
                return prompts.caption_sample(row, seed=draw, scaling=self.scaling)
        return prompts.sample(row, mode=self.mode, scaling=self.scaling)


def collate(batch: list[dict]) -> list[dict]:
    """Pad each sample's series to a whole number of patches; text-only samples have none."""
    if not any(sample["time_series"] for sample in batch):
        return batch
    return extend_time_series_to_match_patch_size_and_aggregate(batch, patch_size=PATCH_SIZE)


def loader(frame: pd.DataFrame, batch_size: int, shuffle: bool, workers: int, mode: str = "series",
           scaling: str = "z", caption_share: float = 0.0) -> DataLoader:
    """A DataLoader over formatted samples."""
    return DataLoader(TripDataset(frame, mode, scaling, caption_share), batch_size=batch_size, shuffle=shuffle, collate_fn=collate,
                      num_workers=workers, persistent_workers=False)

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Nebius job: four one-GPU trip-delay runs side by side on a 4x L40S node.
#
# The bucket mounted at /data is only read (code/trip.tar.gz, code/requirements.txt,
# data/examples.parquet). Bucket mounts may not allow overwriting or appending, so every run
# writes to local disk, prints its progress to the job log with a run prefix (visible with
# `nebius ai job logs <id> --follow`), and the results are copied to /data/runs/$RUN_TAG/ once,
# as new files, when the script exits.
set -uo pipefail

DATA=/data
EXAMPLES=${EXAMPLES:-data/examples.parquet}  # e.g. data/examples_720h.parquet for the long-series build
for required in code/trip.tar.gz code/requirements.txt "$EXAMPLES"; do
  # Fail in seconds, not after the package install, when the bucket is not filled yet.
  [ -f "$DATA/$required" ] || { echo "missing $DATA/$required in the bucket"; exit 1; }
done
WORK=/workspace/trip-run
LOCAL=/workspace/results
OUT="$DATA/runs/${RUN_TAG:-ablations}"
STEPS=${STEPS:-2000}
VAL_LIMIT=${VAL_LIMIT:-3000}
TEST_LIMIT=${TEST_LIMIT:-5000}
GENERATE=${GENERATE:-16}
mkdir -p "$WORK" "$LOCAL"
cd "$WORK"

copy_results() {
  # New files under a fresh prefix only, so no mount has to overwrite or append.
  echo "$(date -u +%FT%TZ) copying results to $OUT"
  mkdir -p "$OUT" && cp -r "$LOCAL/." "$OUT/" && echo "$(date -u +%FT%TZ) results copied"
}
trap copy_results EXIT

export HF_HOME=/workspace/hf
export REDACTED:True
nvidia-smi

# The CUDA runtime image is minimal: fetch curl, then uv, then a Python 3.12 environment
# pinned to the versions the devbox trained with (opentslm needs Python 3.12 or later).
# build-essential: Triton compiles GPU kernels at runtime and needs a C compiler.
apt-get update -qq && apt-get install -y -qq curl ca-certificates build-essential > /dev/null
curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH"
uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
# torch comes from the CUDA 13.0 index, as on the devbox; the rest is pinned from its freeze.
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python torch==2.14.0 torchvision==0.29.0 --index-url https://download.pytorch.org/whl/cu130
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -r "$DATA/code/requirements.txt"

tar -xzf "$DATA/code/trip.tar.gz"
mkdir -p data/trip
cp "$DATA/$EXAMPLES" data/trip/examples.parquet

# Download the base model and both checkpoints once, before four processes race for them.
.venv/bin/python - <<'PY'
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download, snapshot_download
snapshot_download("unsloth/Llama-3.2-3B")
for repo in ("OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-3b-m4-sp", "OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-3b-ecg-sp"):
    hf_hub_download(repo, "model_checkpoint.pt")
print("models cached")

**Why `final-v4-both` finishes around 08:15:** it is the slowest setup we have.
- **Training:** text plus encoder in one prompt needs gradient checkpointing to fit in memory, which makes each step 1.08 s instead of 0.59 s for stacked text. 12,000 steps take 3.6 hours.
- **Scoring:** the full 93,738-trip test adds about another hour.
- **Start:** it was submitted at 03:20.

It isn't the submission candidate; that's `final-v4-text`, due around 06:00.

**On the embeddings, three things:**

1. **A token count, measured on 400 test examples.** Encoder only needs 410 tokens per prompt, text only 844. The encoder packs about 480 number tokens into 45 embeddings, so a prompt is half as long for equal accuracy. We already know encoder-only at 12,000 steps beats XGBoost on May and September at about the text model's level. That is a real TSLM argument, and it matches the brief's "context wall" slide.

2. **Five new ablations, all 2,000 steps on the same data and loss, results around 05:40 to 06:00:**

   | Job | What it shows |
   |---|---|
   | No series at all | The floor |
   | Encoder only | What the embeddings add over no series: the fair "with vs without embeddings" test |
   | Text plus encoder | Directly comparable with the text run we already have |
   | Text plus encoder, 50% modality dropout | During training, half the rows hide the numbers from the text. The model can no longer ignore the encoder because text is easier. |
   | Stacked data, encoder only | Whether 45 embeddings can replace about 480 number tokens in the best model |

   If modality dropout clearly beats text, a longer stacked run with it could still finish before 12:00, though tight.

3. **Other tokenization or loss are unlikely to help the encoder:**
   - **Tokenization:** Llama 3 already writes every number from 0 to 999 as a single token, which the LLMTime paper found to be the recipe that matters.
   - **Loss:** exact-minute cross-entropy plus CRPS is already the best of the three losses we tested; soft targets were worse.
   - **What could make embeddings win outright** needs more than the hours left: series the text can't hold (event-level delays at upstream stations), OpenTSLM's cross-attention variant instead of soft prompts, or a separate alignment stage.

Everything new is committed (`b314020`, `bfd56d9`, `c9ef0da`) and nothing is pushed. Each job now pins its own copy of the code, so the causes subagent can't break them by uploading.

input.prompt:
Research task (web search + reading primary sources; do not edit any files). Verify every citation (authors, venue, year, arXiv ID) by opening the source; say plainly when something could not be verified. Report under 700 words.

## Our setup
OpenTSLM-SoftPrompt (Langer et al., arXiv:2510.02410) on Llama-3.2-3B with LoRA: a small patch encoder (patch size 4, pretrained on M4 via the `OpenTSLM/llama-3.2-3b-m4-sp` checkpoint) plus a linear/MLP projector maps each time series to soft tokens prepended with a short text caption per series. Task: predict a German train's arrival delay (minutes, readout = distribution over number tokens 0..999 after "Answer:", loss = token cross-entropy + CRPS on the minute distribution). Series per example: the train's departure delays at stops so far (2 to 30 values), 30 daily median delays at the target stop, 72 hourly late-shares at the target station, 72 hourly late-shares network-wide (also tried 720 hourly), previous trains' arrival delays at the stop today, planned trajectory channels. Each series z-normalised with mean/std written in the caption (also tried fixed scaling: no change).

Findings so far (2,000 steps unless stated, CRPS on 5,000 test examples):
- Numbers written into the prompt as text beat encoder-only at 2k (2.938 vs 2.994); encoder-only catches up at 12k steps (2.889, level with text at 5k).
- Text + encoder = text (no gain). Random-init encoder = pretrained encoder. Higher encoder LR (5x): no gain. A captioning curriculum (30% of rows are series-reading questions): worse at 2k. Two-stage (encoder-only with LM frozen, then unfreeze): stage 2 reached the text level, no more. 720 h series instead of 72 h: no gain. Trajectory channels: no gain.
- Running now: modality dropout (hide the numbers from text in 50% of both-mode training rows).
- Encoder-only prompts are half the tokens (410 vs 844).
- An XGBoost forecast written into the prompt ("stacking") gives the best model.

## Questions
1. What published techniques make a time-series encoder contribute in LLM-based time-series models (soft prompt / projector / cross-attention), especially when the same information is also available as text? Candidates to check (verify, don't assume): normalisation choices (RevIN, keeping scale via separate level tokens), patch length and multi-scale patching, frequency-domain or learned tokenizers, alignment pretraining (captioning, contrastive text-series alignment, e.g. Time-LLM reprogramming, TEST, ChatTS, Time-MQA, OpenTSLM's curriculum), auxiliary losses (reconstruction/forecasting heads on the encoder, CKA/contrastive), modality dropout / gating, cross-attention (OpenTSLM-Flamingo), encoder freezing schedules, series-as-image (ViTime / vision encoders on plots), number-aware embeddings (xVal, arXiv:2310.02989), etc.
2. Evidence about when encoders help vs text serialisation: series length, noise, number of channels, and any paper that shows encoders winning over text for short series.
3. For probabilistic forecasting with LLMs: losses beyond CE (CRPS, distributional heads, histogram/soft labels, "regression-aware" decoding e.g. RAFT/RAIL), and tokenisation of numbers (digit-level vs single-token numbers).
4. Ways to make more use of time data in context: retrieval of similar past episodes/analog forecasting into the prompt (e.g. retrieval-augmented TS forecasting like RAF / TimeRAF), multi-resolution context, event/calendar covariates.

## Output
A ranked list of the 6 to 10 most promising ideas for OUR setup that can be implemented and tested with a 2,000-step run (about 30 to 45 minutes each on an H100) within the next ~4 hours. For each: one-line mechanism, verified source(s), why it might fix our specific "encoder adds nothing over text" finding, implementation effort (small/medium/large) and risk. Then a short list of ideas that are good but too big for today.

## Context
One example = (train run, target stop, forecast time t0), answer = arrival delay at the target stop. The encoder currently sees: the run's departure delays at stops so far, 30 daily medians at the target stop, 72 (or 720) hourly late-shares at the target station and network-wide, previous trains on the route today at the stop, planned trajectory channels. Which time series, strictly available before t0 (no leakage), could carry information the text cannot hold cheaply and that plausibly predicts this train's delay better? Examine feasibility against the actual data and builder code. Candidates to check (and add your own):
- Downstream stations on this train's remaining route: recent (last 2 to 6 h) delays of other trains at the next k stops / segments (congestion ahead), as series at 15-minute or event resolution.

- The same train number on previous days: its per-stop delay trajectory over the last 14 to 28 days (a matrix of days x stops, flattened or one channel per day), especially delay gained/recovered on the remaining segment.
- Segment-level running-time deviations (actual minus planned running time between consecutive stops) for the remaining segments, recent hours.
- Event-resolution series at the target station (every arrival's delay in the last 3 h, ordered), instead of hourly shares.
- Cancellation / platform-change counts, calendar (hour-of-week profiles).
For each: is it computable from the processed data we have (which columns, how the builder would join it), rough build cost (CPU time for ~300k examples plus the September forward set), series length, whether it overlaps with what the text already has, and a leakage note. Also say how the planned remaining route (stop sequence) is available (`via`, `ppth`, stop pattern columns).

## Output
Rank the top 4 candidate series by (expected signal x feasibility today). For the top 2, give a concrete implementation sketch: which function in the builder to extend, the join logic in pandas/duckdb, and an estimate of wall time to rebuild examples_v4 + forward_v4 with the new channels on the devbox CPU. Deadline context: it is ~05:00 Zurich, submission 12:00, a 2,000-step test run takes ~40 minutes, so anything needing more than ~2 hours to build is out.

content.text:
Research is done and three new encoder experiments are running.

**What we can already show (committed as `1ff911e`):** the time series are what beat XGBoost. The same model without the series ties XGBoost (−0.014, not significant). Series written as text beat that no-series model by 0.054 CRPS overall and 0.101 beyond 30 minutes, both real.

**What the research says:**
- **Literature:** no paper shows a series encoder beating text on short series. A 2026 preprint calls the failure "text collapse": the model reads the easier of two inputs that carry the same information.
- **Fixes it points to:** give the encoder information the text doesn't have, and don't blur the most recent value into a patch of four.
- **Our loss:** the agent found no prior paper that fine-tunes an LLM's number tokens with CRPS, so that part is plausibly new.

**Running from it (2,000 steps each):**
- **Split inputs**, jobs submitted 05:05. The short trajectory stays in the text; the 90-day, station and network history goes only through the encoder. One job on stacked data, one with one value per patch as well.
- **One value per patch**, encoder only, on the original data.
- **New series the text doesn't have.** A subagent is building them on the devbox: this train number's gain from the current stop to the target over the last 28 days, and the trains just ahead on the corridor. XGBoost gets the same features, so the comparison stays fair. It launches a stacked text job and a split job by about 06:45.

**Already running:**
- five encoder ablations, results around 05:40 to 06:00;
- the teammate-causes job;
- the finals: `final-v4-text` about 06:00, `final-v3-both` 07:20, `final-v4-both` 08:15.

content.text:
The new series from the v7 build are the biggest data gain of the night, but they help XGBoost as much as our model. Everything is committed; the latest commit is `92b56e0` and nothing is pushed.

**The two new series:**
- how much delay this train number gained or recovered between the current stop and the target over the last 28 days;
- the trains just ahead on the same corridor.

**The catch:** XGBoost with these series cuts its CRPS by 0.111 on the 5,000 shared test trips, real at every lead time. On the full test it now scores 2.616, which beats our best finished final, `final-v2-text` (2.644). To claim "better than the baseline", the submission model needs these series too, and has to beat this stronger XGBoost.

**What I did about it:**
- **Merged** the builder change into `db-train-model` (`0cc4cd6`) and recorded the new baseline in DESIGN (`92b56e0`).
- **2,000-step tests on the new data**, stacked text and split mode, results around 06:40. They must beat 2.824 on the 5,000 test trips.
- **Long run started without waiting:** `final-v7-text`, stacked text on the new data, 12,000 steps on the full test, submitted 05:24. Results around 09:00, then a September test on the devbox by about 10:00, so it can still become the submission model before 12:00.

**Encoder results so far:**
- **Stacked encoder only** beats XGBoost-v3 by 0.055 with the series as 45 embeddings instead of about 480 number tokens. It trails stacked text by 0.019.
- **Still running:**
  - modality dropout, and text plus encoder (about 05:45);
  - `final-v4-text` (about 06:00);
  - split inputs and one value per patch (about 06:05);
  - no series at 12,000 steps (about 06:10);
  - the causes job (about 06:05).

All encoder routes on the stacked data land within 0.006 of each other, about 0.02 behind stacked text. I'll add this row with the next batch of results.
What do you mean by "stacked" just to be sure?

"Stacked" means XGBoost's own forecast is written into the language model's prompt as one sentence, so the TSLM starts from the statistical forecast and corrects it. The name comes from stacking in machine learning: a second model trained on top of the first model's predictions.

**What the sentence contains:** for each example, XGBoost's median delay, its 10 to 90% range, P(late) and P(cancelled). For example: "A statistical model forecasts +6 min (range 2 to 14), 38% chance of being late, 3% cancelled." This lives in the `examples_v4` (and now `examples_v7`) files, written by `trip/stack.py`.

**Why it isn't leakage:**
- **Training rows** get an out-of-fold forecast: XGBoost is trained on 4/5 of the training data and predicts the remaining fifth, so the model never sees a forecast fitted on its own row.
- **Validation, test and September** get forecasts from an XGBoost that never saw those rows. For September it was trained on May data only.
- **The comparison is fair:** the same XGBoost is the baseline, so "stacked TSLM beats XGBoost" means the language model adds something on top of the forecast it was given.

**How it relates to the other variants:**

| Variant | XGBoost forecast in the prompt |
|---|---|
| Stacked (v4, v7 data) | yes |
| Not stacked (`examples.parquet`, v2, v3) | no, the TSLM predicts on its own |
| Lead-time blend | no; the two forecasts are averaged afterwards with per-lead weights. Different technique. |

Once a model is stacked, the blend picks weight 1.0 for the TSLM: it already contains XGBoost, so there's nothing left to average in.

Two questions: are there other comparisons worth adding, and should we report something more intuitive than CRPS, like the average error ± a spread, for the audience?

**Yes to the audience metrics.** We already report "median error" (on average how many minutes the predicted median is off), but CRPS means nothing to a jury. I'd add, per model and per lead-time bucket:
- **Typical error:** mean absolute error in minutes, plus the median absolute error ("half the trains are within ±X min").
- **Hit rates:** the share of trains predicted within ±1, ±2 and ±5 minutes.
- **Bias:** the mean signed error, whether it predicts too late or too early on average.
- **Spread:** the standard deviation of the error, your "± deviation".
- **Range honesty:** how often the true delay falls inside our 10 to 90% range, which should be about 80%.

These come from prediction files we already have, so there's no new training. I'll write a small script for it.

**Other comparisons worth having**, ranked by value per effort:
1. **Zero-shot model, no fine-tuning.** The same OpenTSLM checkpoint on the same prompts. It shows the training is what makes the difference, which the brief's "adequate TSLM training" criterion asks about. One cheap scoring job, about 20 minutes.
2. **Breakdown by train class** (long-distance, regional, S-Bahn) and by lead time. It comes from existing files and makes a good pitch slide.
3. **Cancellations, honestly:** our cancellation log loss (0.155) is worse than XGBoost's (0.138). Worth saying before a juror spots it.
4. **DB's own live forecast** would be the most compelling baseline ("better than the DB app"), but it needs the raw change feeds rebuilt with timestamps. Not feasible by 12:00, so I'd name it as next work. Persistence, carrying the current delay forward, is the closest proxy we have.

Resamples example ids with replacement and reports the mean difference (A minus B) in CRPS and

"""Errors in minutes that an audience reads at a glance, for several models on the same examples.

CRPS scores the whole distribution but means little outside forecasting. This reports, for the
predicted median of each model: the average and the typical (median) miss in minutes, the share of
trains predicted within 1, 2 and 5 minutes, the bias (positive: predicted too late) with the spread
of the error, and how often the true delay falls inside the 10 to 90% range (80% is honest).
Only examples every model scored are used; cancelled trains are left out, as in the metrics.

    python trip/plain_metrics.py --examples data/trip/examples_v7.parquet \
        --model "XGBoost=out/trip/baselines_v7/xgboost_test.npz" \
        --model "TSLM=out/trip/ablations/v7-text/tslm_test.npz" --by cls
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

import metrics

LOW, HIGH = 1, 17  # the 10% and 90% levels among the 19 quantiles
LEADS = [(0, 15, "up to 15 min"), (15, 30, "15 to 30 min"), (30, 60, "30 to 60 min"),
         (60, 120, "1 to 2 h"), (120, np.inf, "over 2 h")]


def load(spec: str) -> tuple[str, pd.Series, np.ndarray]:
    """Name, example ids and quantiles from a ``name=path.npz`` argument."""
    name, path = spec.split("=", 1)
    with np.load(path) as data:
        return name, pd.Series(data["example_id"]), data["quantiles"]


def summary(y: np.ndarray, q: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, float]:
    """Plain error figures of one model on one group of examples."""
    error = q[:, metrics.MEDIAN] - y
    miss = np.abs(error)
    return {
        "average miss (min)": miss.mean(),
        "typical miss (min)": np.median(miss),
        "within 1 min": (miss <= 1).mean(),
        "within 2 min": (miss <= 2).mean(),
        "within 5 min": (miss <= 5).mean(),
        "bias (min)": error.mean(),
        "spread (min)": error.std(),
        "in 10-90% range": ((y >= q[:, LOW]) & (y <= q[:, HIGH])).mean(),
    }


def table(title: str, y: np.ndarray, models: dict[str, np.ndarray]) -> str:
    """One markdown table: a row per model, a column per figure."""
    rows = {name: summary(y, q) for name, q in models.items()}
    columns = list(next(iter(rows.values())))
    lines = [f"### {title} ({len(y):,} trains)", "", "| Model | " + " | ".join(columns) + " |",
             "|---|" + "---|" * len(columns)]
    for name, row in rows.items():
        cells = [f"{100 * v:.0f}%" if c.startswith(("within", "in ")) else f"{v:+.2f}" if c.startswith("bias")
                 else f"{v:.2f}" for c, v in row.items()]
        lines.append(f"| {name} | " + " | ".join(cells) + " |")
    return "\n".join(lines) + "\n"


def main() -> None:
    """Print the tables: overall, by lead time, and optionally by train class."""
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser()
    parser.add_argument("--model", action="append", required=True, help="name=path.npz, repeatable")
    parser.add_argument("--examples", default="data/trip/examples.parquet")
    parser.add_argument("--by", choices=["lead", "cls"], action="append", default=None,
                        help="extra breakdowns; lead time is always included")
    args = parser.parse_args()

    loaded = [load(spec) for spec in args.model]
    shared = set(loaded[0][1])
    for _, ids, _ in loaded[1:]:
        shared &= set(ids)
    frame = pd.read_parquet(args.examples, columns=["example_id", "target_minutes", "cancelled", "lead_minutes", "cls"])
    frame = frame[frame["example_id"].isin(shared) & ~frame["cancelled"]].reset_index(drop=True)
    y = frame["target_minutes"].to_numpy(dtype=np.float64)
    models = {}
    for name, ids, quantiles in loaded:
        row_of = pd.Series(np.arange(len(ids)), index=ids.to_numpy())
        models[name] = quantiles[row_of.loc[frame["example_id"]].to_numpy()]

    print(table("All trains", y, models))
    for low, high, label in LEADS:
        keep = ((frame["lead_minutes"] > low) | (low == 0)) & (frame["lead_minutes"] <= high)
        if keep.any():
            print(table(f"Planned arrival {label} away", y[keep], {n: q[keep.to_numpy()] for n, q in models.items()}))
    if args.by and "cls" in args.by:
        for cls, group in frame.groupby("cls"):
            keep = frame["cls"].eq(cls).to_numpy()
            print(table(f"{cls} trains", y[keep], {n: q[keep] for n, q in models.items()}))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

content.text:
Yes to both. I added the plain-minutes numbers and started the most useful extra comparison.

**Numbers in minutes** (committed as `083100e`, script `trip/plain_metrics.py`, new section 5.5 in EVALUATION). Full test, 88,479 trains:

| Model | Average miss | Within 1 min | Within 2 min | Within 5 min | Truth inside 10 to 90% range |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Persistence | 3.75 min | 62% | 72% | 86% | 84% |
| XGBoost (combined features) | 3.41 min | 57% | 71% | 85% | 82% |
| XGBoost (plus new series) | 3.28 min | 59% | 72% | 86% | 82% |
| TSLM text final 12k | 3.32 min | **65%** | **75%** | **87%** | 90% |

- **Best pitch line:** the model predicts 65% of trains to within a minute, against 57 to 59% for XGBoost. It wins in every train class (S-Bahn 85% vs 77% on the 5,000 test trains) and in every lead-time bucket.
- **Mean ± deviation doesn't work here.** The spread is 10 to 13 minutes for every model, driven by a few very long delays none of them foresees. "Within X minutes" is clearer.
- **Honest notes:**
  - All models predict slightly too early on average.
  - Our 10 to 90% range is a bit too wide (about 90% vs the 80% target), cautious rather than overconfident.
  - On average minutes, the new XGBoost with the extra series (3.28) edges our older 12k final (3.32). The v7 models (2,000 steps) beat it: 3.45 vs 3.51 on the 5,000 test trains.

**Extra comparisons:**
1. **Zero-shot, running:** the same model and prompts without fine-tuning, on the same 5,000 test trains (submitted 06:11). It shows the training is what makes it work.
2. **Class and lead-time breakdown:** done, in the tables above.
3. **Cancellations:** worth naming openly. Our cancellation log loss is worse than XGBoost's (0.155 vs 0.138).
4. **DB's own live forecast:** the most convincing baseline, but it needs a rebuild of the raw feeds. Not feasible by 12:00, so it goes under next steps.
